results.title: Mysteel月报：9月算力市场高位震荡_我的钢铁网
highlights:
```
8月国内GPU算力租赁市场高位震荡，品种分化加剧。H100包月价格先抑后扬，月末报16.07元/卡/时；H800冲高回落，振幅达48%。供给端H200放量、B300期货入市重塑高端定价；国产昇腾910B交易活跃度提升。产业端天猫上线AI空间站等事件表明推理算力需求扩张。展望9月，高端卡价格上方空间收窄，H100若回落至13元以下具配置价值；推理端及国产算力为关注主线。
```

概述： 8月国内GPU算力租赁市场整体震荡走强，型号间分化显著加剧。H800单卡按需全月振幅达48%，中旬一度冲高至16.02元/卡/时后回落至月末10.81元/卡/时。H100单卡包月价格先抑后扬，月初12.80元/卡/时下探至10.91元/卡/时后反弹至16.07元/卡/时。A系列和H20等中端品种走势平稳，消费级GPU维持窄幅震荡格局。

供给端，H200五年闭口大单持续放量，月租从12.5万元/台探至11.6万元/台区间；B300期货入市定价，高端算力定价格局面临重塑。国产算力端，昇腾910B走势平稳。

产业端，英伟达拟收购Hugging Face、DeepSeek上调API定价、国家电投与中国联通签署算电协同协议、天猫上线AI空间站——系列事件表明从芯片到模型到应用的算力需求全链条正在扩张，推理算力有望成为下一阶段主要增量来源。

...

H100 80G包月价格月初短暂拉升至17.33元/卡/时后急速回落至10.91元/卡/时，此后持续盘整，月末最后一周企稳反弹至16.07元/卡/时，整体呈现震荡走强趋势。H100 80G按需价格走势类似，当月报收15.58元/卡/时。两者均表明高端训练卡在10-12元/卡/时区间存在较强支撑。

H800 80G本月波动同样较大。月初13.59元/卡/时，中旬连续拉升触及16.02元/卡/时高点，下旬快速回落至10.81元/卡/时，全月振幅达48%。波动主要受大模型训练需求的脉冲式释放驱动——需求集中释放时段价格冲高，冷却后迅速回落。

...

A系列8月走势整体平稳。 A800 80G单卡按需月初6.19元/卡/时，全月区间5.94-6.30元/卡/时，月末收于6.15元/卡/时，整体走势平稳。A800 40G按需全月小幅波动，最高2.22元/卡/时，月末回落至2.14元/卡/时。A100 80G包月月初6.63元/卡/时，8月4日探底6.25元/卡/时，月末6.59元/卡/时，整体承压。A100 40G包月月初2.49元/卡/时，中旬下探至2.32元/卡/时后修复至2.60元/卡/时。A100 40G按需从2.72元/卡/时小幅拉升至3.04元/卡/时后企稳。

...

消费级GPU走势分化明显。RTX 5090受供应偏紧影响自8月低点累计上涨约3%。RTX 4090月初受英伟达停产预期影响，部分区域一度拉涨，但后续快速回落至2元/卡/时附近企稳。

...

高端训练卡方面，京津冀与长三角报价维持高位，其他地区相对较低，A100 80G包月京津冀7.52元/卡/时，显著高于成渝的5.31元/卡/时，价差约41.6%。消费级卡方面，粤港澳RTX 4090报2.50元/卡/时，成渝1.91元/卡/时，价差约30.9%，主要受区域终端需求结构差异影响。

1、 H200、H800供给放量，价格中枢下移

8月H200租赁市场供给显著增加。新疆128台五年闭口12.5万元/台/月，贵州128台五年闭口11.6万元/台/月，山东、甘肃128-512台五年闭口11.75万元/台/月，广东128台五年闭口12万元/台/月。从报价走势看，租赁价格中枢维持在12万元/台/月左右。市场同期出现千台H200集采大单报盘，此外还有H800 PCIE版32台新疆现货1-3年闭口可租，H100 128台三年闭口租金7.7万元/台/月。

2、 B300期货入市定价

B300期货本月报盘规模扩大，市场正在形成初步定价基准。DELL B300 3T 128台期货报价920万元/台，超微B300 4T 128台期货租金22.8-23万元/台/月，技嘉B300 3T 32台现货已抵达深圳保税仓，报价1380万元/台。三个品牌定价逻辑各异，B300的价格锚点仍在博弈中，预计未来1-2个月逐步清晰。B300入市将对高端算力定价格局产生结构性影响。

3、 国产算力：交易活跃度提升

国产算力本月最值得关注的是交易量而非价格。昇腾910B 32G单卡包月成渝区域报0.51元/卡/时，全月走势平稳。同期西北地区出现32台910B2三年闭口的求租需求和32台一年闭口的求租需求，其他地区出现125台910B4求租需求。国产卡性价比的吸引力在持续积累，需求不断扩大。

...

本月出现若干值得关注的信号：天猫上线AI空间站，集合阿里云、智谱、Kimi等头部大模型订阅服务，支持按周期订阅和按用量付费两种模式，算力消费正从企业级采购向个人订阅跨越；阿里发布Qoder智能体工作台，用户以自然语言即可完成编码开发，内置40余个连接器和70余个插件，AI原生开发工具的普及将进一步推高推理端算力消耗；DeepSeek计划大幅上调API定价，光环新网算力业务收入突破20亿元并计划年底前将GPU持有量从2万张扩至6万张。这些信号共同指向一个判断：AI算力的需求驱动力正从训练主导向"训练+推理双轮驱动"转变，推理端的长尾需求正在规模化涌现。

四、后市展望

展望9月，国内GPU算力租赁市场面临供需两端的结构性变化。

高端训练卡价格中枢仍有支撑但上方空间收窄。H100、H800受国际租金上行和国产替代需求支撑，价格难以大幅下行，但H200五年闭口放量和B300期货入市将逐步形成价格锚定效应，对H100、H800的高价区间构成边际压力。H100包月若回落至13元/卡/时以下，将是较好的配置窗口。

推理算力正从预期转化为实际需求。天猫AI空间站、阿里Qoder等平台的上线，叠加DeepSeek涨价和光环新网扩卡等信号，表明推理端算力消耗正在从"企业级"向"消费级"渗透。RTX 5090供不应求的局面短期难以缓解，消费级推理卡的价格弹性将持续释放。

国产算力渗透加速但尚未形成规模替代。昇腾910B系列交易活跃度提升明显，价格具备显著竞争力，但在高端场景的生态适配仍需时间。算电协同政策推动下，中西部"绿电+国产卡"模式有望形成差异化优势。

后续需持续关注的变量包括：头部互联网厂商下季度训练、推理需求释放节奏；H200、H800区域间现货调拨对头部按需订单的传导；B300期货定价体系的成熟度；国产算力性价比突破的节点；国际AI云提价对国内价格的时滞效应。

总体而言，当前算力租赁市场处于放量博弈的中期阶段。长期延续需求扩张趋势。对于采购方，建议在H系列价格回调时锁定中长期合同；对于投资方，推理端算力布局和国产算力市场渗透是两条值得重点跟踪的主线。

results.title: Jensen Huang Says a 22% Rent Jump Proves Old Nvidia Chips Keep Earning
highlights:
## Key takeaways

- Huang says a 22% jump in chip rental prices proves AI hardware keeps earning.
- The three-year-old Nvidia chip now rents for $3.28 an hour.
- The same chip once cost $7 to $8 an hour.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says rising AI chip rental prices prove that older hardware keeps earning, after rates for a three-year-old chip climbed 22% in a month.

The chip is the H100, the training processor behind the first wave of generative AI. It now rents for $3.28 an hour. Huang calls that durability. The longer record complicates the claim.

Index data circulated on X puts the hourly rate at $3.28, a gain of roughly 22% over the past month. Huang shared the chart and described Nvidia compute as fungible, durable, and revenue-generating.

> NVIDIA compute is fungible, durable and highly rentable. ... https://t.co/cvmjaNoiK8
> 
> — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) September 8, 2026

...

The rebound cuts against standard accounting. Hyperscalers write down graphics processing units (GPUs) over roughly five to six years. Michael Burry argues the real useful life runs shorter, and he expanded his Nvidia short in late August.

## Why One Month Does Not Settle the Depreciation Debate

History cuts both ways here. On-demand capacity for the same chip once cost $7 to $8 an hour at large cloud providers, and early rates ran higher still. Against that base, $3.28 remains a steep markdown.

Supply also explains part of the move. Newer Blackwell systems stay reserved for the biggest buyers, so older clusters keep filling inference workloads. Tight power and memory keep the whole market expensive.

Then there is who pays the rent. CoreWeave, a cloud firm that buys Nvidia chips and rents them out, carried $35 billion of debt at the end of June. Nvidia, meanwhile, agreed to rent back unused capacity from such partners. Critics count that among the off-balance-sheet AI deals that flatter demand.

results.title: Nvidia's 3-Year-Old H100 Chip Is Still Getting the Market to Pay Up, Jensen Huang Says Compute Is 'Fungible, Durable and Highly Rentable'
highlights:
On Monday, Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ: NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang doubled down on his view that AI computing hardware is becoming a valuable, financeable asset as rental prices for the company's older H100 GPUs continue to climb. 

## Huang Calls Nvidia Compute a 'Revenue-Generating Asset' 

"NVIDIA compute is fungible, durable and highly rentable," Huang wrote in a post on X. "It is a productive, revenue-generating asset." 

> NVIDIA compute is fungible, durable and highly rentable. It is a productive, revenue-generating asset. https://t.co/cvmjaNoiK8 
> 
> — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) September 8, 2026 

His comments came in response to Ornn Exchange, which said its Compute Price Index showed the rental price for Nvidia's three-year-old H100 had climbed 22% in a month to $3.28 per hour. 

> The H100 is a three-year-old training chip. Its rental price is up 22 percent on the month, to $3.28 an hour. Every depreciation schedule assumes a chip this old only loses value. The market is paying up for it instead. pic.twitter.com/TNSqgys3vx 
> 
> — Ornn (@OrnnExchange) September 7, 2026 

The increase is notable because conventional depreciation models generally assume that older hardware loses value over time. Strong demand for AI computing, however, is helping some Nvidia GPUs maintain or even increase their rental economics.

...

## Why Rising H100 Rental Prices Matter 

The economics matter for Nvidia's financing strategy. 

If GPUs can consistently generate revenue through rentals, investors and lenders can potentially assess them more like productive infrastructure than conventional depreciating equipment. 

However, Ben Emons, founder of FedWatch Advisors, views China as the biggest threat to Huang's push. 

In August, Emons cautioned that China's rapidly growing domestic AI computing capacity could eventually flood the market with cheaper chips, sparking a price war that could weaken the value of Nvidia GPUs used as collateral. 

Last year, legendary short-seller Jim Chanos warned that a critical accounting issue involving Nvidia chips could pose a "massive financial risk" to companies aggressively investing in the sector.

results.title: A new market for AI compute: What GPU futures could mean for energy — Energy Gang — EnergyPod
highlights:
## Overview

- CME Group and Silicon Data are launching Compute Futures, a futures contract for GPU computing capacity.
- The core debate is whether this new market can bring price stability and transparency to GPU rental costs, which are closely tied to volatile energy prices.
- Who should listen? Energy traders, data center investors, lenders financing AI infrastructure, and power company planners deciding where to build generation for data centers.

## Key Takeaways

- CME Group and Silicon Data are building a futures contract for GPU rental prices. It's financially settled against a Silicon Data index tracking NVIDIA's H100 chip, built by Carmen Li (Silicon Data's founder and CEO, who also runs a GPU procurement platform called ComputeChange).
- The potential market size is enormous. Carmen Li says derivatives markets typically run 10 to 15 times bigger than the spot market; spot GPU spending was $300 billion last year and is $2 trillion this year, implying a derivatives market that could reach roughly $30 trillion.
- This market is developing far faster than normal. Peter Keavey says building a futures market usually takes 10 to 15 years, but this one is being compressed into about 3 years because AI's investment cycle moves so fast.
- Energy is the single biggest variable in GPU pricing. Keavey says power costs are the most volatile input, so a Compute Futures contract lets users hedge GPU costs alongside gas and power prices.
- An exchange adds three core benefits over today's private deals. Keavey lists a clearinghouse that removes counterparty risk, a centralized order book that builds liquidity, and transparent benchmark pricing that creates forward price curves.
- The contract mirrors how GPU capacity is actually rented today. It prices per hour per chip, using an average of 730 hours in a month, and futures will initially be listed out 36 months (versus oil's 10 to 15 years).
- GPU rental prices have already swung wildly. Rates hit $7 to $10 an hour at the peak of chip scarcity in 2023-2024, fell to $2 to $3 an hour as supply normalized, and Nvidia's B200 chip price dropped before rising back above its original price this year.
- The supplier market exploded in just a few years. Carmen Li says there were only three or four neocloud providers when she started tracking the market three years ago; now there are more than 200 globally.
- Lenders and investors are a major expected source of demand. Banks financing data center construction want forward price curves the way they already use them for oil project lending, and some investors want direct exposure to GPU compute, similar to investing in gold rather than a gold miner.
- Energy companies have a stake even without trading GPU contracts. Keavey says power producers deciding whether to build baseload generation for data centers, in regions like Texas or Virginia, can use futures pricing signals to guide where and whether to invest.
- AI's uncertain growth curve is the market's biggest open question. Carmen Li cites Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's "five layers of cake" image (GPU, token, and model layers) to explain why compute demand is hard to predict, and she calls the overall market a "giant baby" still in its early days.

（3）亚康股份签订11.88亿元算力租赁大单

据The Information报道，CoreWeave等数据中心运营商议价筹码正在上升，合同条款天平开始向供给侧倾斜。英伟达及AMD入场竞标为客户提供信用担保，最长可达15年。

预计明日中端训练卡价格仍有上行空间，高端训练卡及消费级显卡维持窄幅震荡格局。

results.title: The Rise of Compute Capital Markets | Pantera
highlights:
Compute and datacenter infrastructure spend has become a trillion dollar category, rivalling US consumption as a major pillar of US economic growth. Yet, for all this demand for compute as AI agents trickle into the real world economy, the process of actually acquiring GPUs is surprisingly old-school. While marketplaces like SF Compute, Vast AI, and Runpod all exist, much of the actual buying and selling of GPU nodes is actually run through a collection of group chats, over-the-counter (OTC) brokers, and bespoke bilateral agreements.

Today, GPU compute is still early in its financialization lifecycle [1]. Like electricity, compute is not a totally fungible asset – it is bound by the constraints of SKU, time, and location. But fast forward 5-10 years, compute may well be come a commodity asset just like power or oil – a critical global resource underpinning economic output in the AI era. In this essay, we will investigate the process of how this occurs – what are the lessons from electricity that we can take to understand compute markets structure, the landscape of products being built in the space, as well as both the opportunities and open questions of commoditizing compute.

...

Today, the inference stack can be largely be seen as a having three distinct layers that form the structural longs and shorts for compute:

1. Neocloud layer: players such as Nebius, Coreweave, and others operate physical datacenters and form the sell-side for GPUs.
2. On-tap layer: developer platforms such as Fireworks and Baseten then take these baremetal environments into “rich” GPU environments that a developer can run tasks or get inference tokens on-tap. This layer is a buy-side for GPUs.
3. Application layer: applications such as Cursor, Perplexity, Rime etc. make use of these inference platforms to deliver an end-product to users and businesses. This layer is a buy-side for tokens (which in-turn requires GPUs)

While each player in this ecosystem has their own slightly different strategy of managing GPUs, largely speaking the neoclouds are the structural short-side for the GPU markets, whereas the on-tap and application layers are the long-side. On the other hand, a hyperscalar such as Amazon or Google operates different inhouse products at every layer of this stack. As for the “margin flow,” a rule of thumb is that when one of the top-layer apps spends $100 in tokens, ~$45 goes to the on-tap layer, and $50 to the neocloud/GPU layer. The remaining $5 is on a routing layer such as OpenRouter.

...

1. Managing Inflation: the analog of “inflation” in the GPU economy is arguably the depreciation cycle, especially relative to SOTA chips. By being able to control product releases (eg. Vera Rubin), NVIDIA is able to have some degree of influence over how quickly or slowly GPUs depreciate over time.
2. Full Employment: NVIDIA wants “full employment” of its GPUs – if utilization of GPUs are very high (due to high demand for tokens), this means that people will want to buy more units of its GPUs. Therefore NVIDIA is also incentivized to increase the financialization and make GPU-hours more liquid, such that its utilization can increase.
3. Be a lender of last resort: NVIDIA has also announced that it will provide up to 25% residual value support, which can be seen as a form of bailout/insurance guarantee of GPU value in the case that neoclouds and other GPU providers run into liquidity crunches.

...

Product 1 – Physical Settlement. This refers to the process of actually delivering physical GPU units to the end consumers that actually need them, and includes players such as SF Compute, Hyperbolic, Vast, Runpod, Compute Exchange. This is the product layer closest to the metal and actually interfacing with the AI principals mentioned above. Because of the heterogeneity in compute SKUs, many players here start out simply as brokers, taking commission on matching GPU demand with individual neoclouds [8]. Eventually, the end goal here is some form of a “spot exchange” for compute, but consistently controlling for quality at the physical delivery of the GPU metal is actually a hard problem, especially for players whose supply comes from a decentralized network. It is possible that for this layer to mature, we need to see a Moody’s like ratings agency that guarantees the quality of the underlying deliverable.

...

However, today there still is an extremely large spread between many of the compute indices and the individual GPU marketplaces. There may be two key factors to this price differential. Firstly, there is dispersion in the underlying product, as there is a huge difference in product reliability, interruptibility, and contract terms across each platform. Secondly, because the orderbooks underneath all of these different compute indices are different, and there is no transparency mandate here in the same way that there is for other asset classes (eg. FERC mandates for power). Many of these compute indices today are simply buying orderbook data in bulk from neoclouds or doing partnerships/revshares to bootstrap the underlying datasets. Moreover, the index layer in and of itself is hard to monetize compared to the exchange and physical settlement layers. Thus, despite being able to make for splashy announcements and being an important layer in the compute markets stack, the index layer alone faces a double-squeeze from both the physical layer (from which it sources prices from) and from the exchange layer (which demands a revenue cut).

results.title: Two months ago the story was that datacenter GPU rental prices were holding flat while consumer cards slid. | Mercatus AI | The Open Intelligence Exchange
highlights:
Two months ago the story was that datacenter GPU rental prices were holding flat while consumer cards slid.

That flipped over the summer.

Cloud rental price per GPU-hour across 30+ providers, September 8:

B300 $8.89 (+5.7% since July 6)
AMD MI300X $4.99 (+6.4%)
H100 $3.85 (+4.6%)
H200 $4.54 (+3.7%)
B200 $6.42 (+1.7%)
A100 80GB $2.04 (flat)
RTX 5090 $0.70 (-1.4%)
RTX 4090 $0.49 (-2.0%)

Every current-generation datacenter GPU got more expensive to rent. The A100 held. Consumer cards kept slipping.

The spread is the point. The gap between an H100 and an RTX 4090 rental was $3.18/hr in July. It is $3.36/hr today. Capacity that can run production inference is getting pricier relative to capacity that cannot.

Nvidia’s H100 AI accelerator is four years old, but its rental price is moving in the opposite direction from its age.

Cloud rental prices for the H100 rose 21.89% in the past month, according to AI computing financial trading platform Ornn. Nvidia released the accelerator in September 2022.

Demand for older products has increased because supplies of newer AI accelerators have failed to keep up with demand. As a result, users are also turning to the H100 for AI computing capacity.

results.title: Anthropic Just Committed $80B in Five Days. Here Is Who It Is Renting From.
highlights:
Recently, two little-known cloud companies reportedly received $80 billion in compute contracts from Anthropic: a six-year, $45 billion agreement with Nscale and a $35 billion agreement with Lambda.

Frontier AI labs are reaching beyond Amazon, Microsoft, and Google to secure the compute they need. This class of company barely existed 3 years ago, but is now forecast to approach $400B in revenue by 2031.

They are called neoclouds and have become a growing share of the compute that frontier labs run on by owning GPU capacity and renting access to it, either by the hour or under a long-term contract.

...

Instead of buying and operating the underlying infrastructure themselves, customers can rent compute from shared infrastructure, an approach known as “pooling.” For more than 15 years, the hyperscalers dominated this business model through AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Most non-AI workloads still work this way today.

But AI workloads require a different approach. Traditional clouds were built heavily on CPUs, but training AI models requires a different type of chip. The most common, industry-standard option is the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU).

A traditional cloud keeps its hardware busy by spreading thousands of smaller jobs across a shared pool. In contrast, AI training runs occupy thousands of GPUs in lockstep for weeks, leaving far less capacity to share.

Packing those GPUs together also raises rack power from roughly 10 to 15 kilowatts to 40 to 250 kilowatts, which requires new networking, electrical systems, and often liquid cooling. AI workloads changed both the chips and the building foundation around it.

Neoclouds solves this by bringing together power, data center infrastructure, and GPUs, and removing unnecessary software layers to maximize raw performance. This grants them two structural advantages.

First, by being built specifically for AI, neoclouds can offer on-demand GPU hours 50-70% below hyperscaler list prices. Second, neoclouds get earlier access to scarce Nvidia GPUs. While the hyperscalers split their GPU purchases with the development of their own chips, Nvidia has a strategic incentive to support neoclouds. By allocating chips and even capital to neoclouds, Nvidia expands its market access and reduces concentration risk.

...

The contracts make the demand story easy to see, but a big question to answer is whether the economics survive the massive, continuous buildout. The counterargument is that neoclouds borrow billions at a premium to buy depreciating hardware, then rent it to customers that are also building their own capacity and custom chips.
